messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Darkness: Dark spaces, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan is a 61-year-old South Asian man who has worked as a paramedic for over three decades, a career he once described as his calling. He is married and, by most outward measures, presents as composed and professionally seasoned. He was referred for psychological assessment following a period of escalating distress that his wife had noticed over the preceding eight months, and which Rajan himself had struggled to name until recently.

The incident that precipitated his current difficulties occurred during a routine emergency call to an industrial facility. Rajan and his partner arrived to find a worker collapsed in a poorly ventilated storage area where a chemical coolant had been leaking for hours. The smell was sharp and medicinal — something between antiseptic and industrial solvent — and the space was dim, lit only by a single emergency strip light that cast long shadows across the floor. Rajan entered without full respiratory protection, a decision made in seconds under pressure, and within minutes he felt his eyes burning, his chest tightening, and a wave of disorientation that he initially mistook for exertion. It was only when he stumbled and his partner dragged him out that he understood something was wrong. He spent two days in hospital under observation. The medical team reassured him that there had been no lasting physiological damage, but Rajan left with something they could not measure on a chart.

In the weeks that followed, the memory did not settle. It remained close to the surface, and certain things could bring it back without any warning at all — not gradually, but instantaneously and in full. The smell of rubbing alcohol on a colleague's hands, the particular quality of darkness in an unlit stairwell, the ambient sounds and smells of the ambulance bay itself: any of these could collapse the distance between then and now, returning him not to a recollection but to the experience itself, complete with the same terror he had felt on the floor of that storage room. When the memory returned this way, the emotional force of it was so overwhelming that he would have to stop whatever he was doing — mid-sentence, mid-task — unable to continue until the wave passed. Because the memory could be triggered without warning, Rajan began to experience his own workplace as a source of constant latent threat, and the ambulance, the bay, the equipment — things he had once handled with ease — became charged with the possibility of re-exposure.

It was the triggers themselves that began to organise his behaviour. To manage the risk of being ambushed by the memory at work, he started avoiding anything that might concentrate the exposure: he declined calls that involved hospitals when he could, found reasons to step back from physical examinations, and felt a creeping dread whenever a shift began. At the same time, the memory's capacity to overwhelm him when it surfaced led him to a strategy that felt, at first, like simple practicality: he made sure he was never alone. He filled every available space in his day with conversation, company, noise — surrounding himself with people so that the silence in which the memory tended to find him could not take hold. His wife noticed that he no longer sat quietly in the evenings, that he sought her company with an urgency that was different from affection. But the constant socialising, while it suppressed the memory's immediate return, also prevented him from processing what had happened, and so the memory remained unintegrated — ready to be triggered again by the next encounter with darkness, or the sharp chemical note of alcohol, or the interior of the vehicle he drove to work each day. The avoidance of medical settings, similarly, foreclosed any opportunity to build a different relationship with the context of the event, keeping the workplace and its associated cues perpetually threatening. Over months, the loop tightened: the triggers fed the memory, the memory sharpened his vigilance toward triggers, and the strategies that were meant to contain both instead preserved them.

He also found himself returning, in quiet moments that broke through despite his efforts, to the question of what he should have done differently — rehearsing the decision not to wait for full equipment, turning it over without resolution. This rumination, though not the centre of his distress, sat beneath everything else.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a near-miss at work: he froze at the entrance to a darkened corridor during a call, and his partner had to take over. He is most afraid, he says, that he has become unreliable — that the person he has been for thirty years is no longer there. What he hopes for, more quietly, is to be able to walk into a dark room without bracing for the floor to disappear beneath him.
